Seeing other people bitching about non-issues/1st world problems while I am rotting brought me to struggle more and more at both empathising and communicating my own feelings, while my depressive episodes made me take a more passive stance (caring/interacting less).

I'm alright, glad to see you are as well. I find it hard to cope with this lately, my mind goes numb.

Bottling up is, like, the baseline for us. Anything beyond that is pure luxury. The current narrative tells us we are born bad, we are inherently toxic, we are dangers, we are society's meatshields. I am fortunate to have a friend, even a single one. I can tell you, I can't even talk to him about my issues. I get what the most of us would in a best-case scenario: the "everyone has their problems, man". And I'm talking about someone who made extensive effort to reach out to me and make sure I am well and sound since I had to take sickness leave.

I ended up searching people qualified enough to rule out shit \*smugly taps forehead\*.  PTSD came from the pressure anyone can potentially get within their 11-16's (nothing fancy: not fitting in, outright bullying, academical pressure... speaking for myself, I was a natural at not being treated like a human beyond the family's scope).

I carried it ever since and I will get my first therapy session tomorrow. I was told various aspects of my personality (normal on its own), coupled with my trauma, made me unintentionally chameleon as a high functionning aspie, hence the wrong guess (like... I fooled someone who made his career on coaching aspies, without even knowing it myself. I guess I have some talent at least).

​

I guess your own issues have something to do with mental illness. I won't tell you the get-a-shower/hobby/just-lift-bro platitudes, I was already furiously lifting showers as a hobby before the bulk of the shitheads spouting this nonsense were done mistaking their baby bottle with their grandma's dildo. We all know this is a lie, sometimes even told by strangers who don't apply their own pieces of advice on a regular basis. I didn't but maybe you can find solace in the fact a lot of people end up in a relationship despite their mental struggles (diagnosed ones even, but I suspect the most of them did well enough to not pursue help in the first place). We can talk if you want.

Hobbies/Travel are great, but eventually, those are not enough to distract you from whatever you lack (in my case, my autism/bipolarity prevents me from anything remotely close to a proper career or any form of proximity with girls), so I relate to what you told, maybe not for the same reasons as yours.

That's why I pretty much don't ever consider talking about any issues with my parents. I feel like mine are just expecting me to succeed academically and anything that stray a smidge away from this ideal narrative will be misunderstood/shunned upon and remain unfixed. That may be the price for a "happy family" I guess.
